terra.problem: The text does not say the whole nation moved into the hills or that staying out of sight was the reason for the shelters.
The passage does not say the Israelites were not behind city walls. It also gives no details about Jericho's walls.
The text does not establish where the Israelites started or say they did not go to the riverbank.
The passage does not say none of what Israel planted ever made it to the table.
The answer is about counting produce, but the explanation switches to counting Midianites and camels without a meaningful connection.
The claim about priests having work for God is outside this passage and has no reference.
Gideon's not seeing the assignment coming is presented as a fact, though the text does not say it.
Papa Dorin was bought from the 25-cent bin; he was called to his mission from the drawer, not hired out of the bin.
Weakest is not the opposite of largest, and the passage does not say how a large clan would have affected Gideon's case.
The text does not say Gideon gives every reason he can think of.
The text does not explicitly identify the fire and offering as the sign Gideon requested.
Gideon asks for a sign, but the text does not specify that he is asking for something visible rather than something to read.
The explanation defines the requested sign as something Gideon can see, though he does not specify that.
The passage does not explicitly call the fire the sign Gideon requested.
The claim that water comes from a rock elsewhere in the Bible needs a reference.
The text does not say the rock stayed in one piece; it leaves the rock's condition unstated.
The passage does not say the angel was standing or that the rock was still glowing.
The passage does not establish that Gideon only realized who the angel was after he vanished.
The identification of Abraham as the father of Israel's people is outside the passage and is not established by the reference given.
The passage identifies the altar as belonging to Gideon's father, but does not locate it at home or in a backyard.
The text does not say the oak stays where it is; it simply does not say Gideon cuts it down.
The passage says to use the pole's wood for the offering, but does not say none of it went to waste.
The text does not say that no one in the city had a quiet morning.
Joash responds to the men, but the passage does not explicitly say whether Gideon was handed over afterward.
The passage does not say the crowd left, or that they left without Gideon.
Joash says Baal should contend for himself with the one who tore down his altar; the passage does not limit that challenge to speaking up.
